aiAgentFacts.fact: In 188 healthy dogs of four breeds, NO differences in echocardiographic variables, NT-proBNP or whole blood taurine were found between grain-free and grain-inclusive diets.
Dogs eating grain-free diets had higher median high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (0.076 vs 0.048 ng/mL, P<.001), which the authors state MIGHT indicate low-level cardiomyocyte injury.

Dogs eating diets with peas, lentils or potatoes in the top 10 ingredients had higher median hs-cTnI (0.059 vs 0.048 ng/mL, P=.006) and more ventricular premature complexes during examination (10% vs 2%, P=.04).
Plasma taurine was HIGHER, not lower, in dogs eating grain-free diets (125 vs 104 nmol/mL, P=.02) — this study found no evidence of diet-induced taurine deficiency in healthy dogs.
The grain-free group comprised only 26 of 188 dogs, so all grain-free comparisons rest on a small subgroup.

In a separate 2018 case series, 23 of 24 golden retrievers with taurine deficiency and DCM were fed grain-free, legume-rich, or combined diets; 23 of 24 improved echocardiographically after diet change plus taurine supplementation.
The Kaplan case series has no control group and applied diet change and taurine supplementation together, so their individual contributions cannot be separated.
Taurine-deficient DCM (Kaplan) and the healthy-dog biomarker findings (Adin) describe different populations and different questions; conflating them is a common error when this topic is summarised.
aiAgentFacts.sourcePaper: Adin et al. 2021; Kaplan et al. 2018

historyQuestions: Supported by both papers' exposure definitions: a complete diet history — brand, specific formulation, top-10 ingredients, and dates of every change, including treats — rather than a binary grain-free/grain-inclusive label.
redFlags: Not defined by these studies. Exercise intolerance, cough, syncope and collapse are the clinical signs that prompt cardiac investigation in the wider literature, not findings of these papers.
differentialDiagnosesMentioned: Taurine-deficient DCM is distinguished from DCM occurring without taurine deficiency; genetic DCM in predisposed breeds is a separate entity these studies do not evaluate.
recommendedDiagnosticWorkups: The studies' own measures: echocardiography, hs-cTnI, NT-proBNP, and whole blood plus plasma taurine. Neither paper proposes a screening protocol for dogs on any particular diet.

limitations: Cross-sectional observational design with owner-chosen diets — no randomisation, and unmeasured confounding by owner characteristics cannot be excluded
Grain-free group was only 26 dogs of 188; all grain-free comparisons rest on that small subgroup
Troponin is an intermediate marker, not a clinical outcome; no dog was followed to determine whether elevated hs-cTnI predicted subsequent disease
All dogs had normal echocardiograms — the study describes healthy dogs, not dogs with DCM
Four breeds only (Doberman Pinscher, Golden Retriever, Miniature Schnauzer, Whippet), several selected for known cardiac profiles; transfer to other breeds is unestablished
Kaplan et al. is an uncontrolled case series of 24 dogs with combined interventions; it establishes association and clinical improvement, not causation
The mechanism connecting non-traditional diets to canine cardiac change remains unidentified in both papers; taurine deficiency explains only a subset of reported cases
